$$
\Delta x=\dfrac{b-a}{n}=\dfrac{2-0}{4}=0.5.
$$

Now, let's sketch our situation. We are using a left Riemann sum, which means we draw the rectangles so that the left corner of each rectangle coincides with the curve.

![](images/56/56427bec8108b822c4e1980725073cedc9fc79575d606014f72ea6ca9f8959c2.png)

The area $\mathcal{A}$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\mathcal A\approx(\overbrace{{\color{red}{f(0)}}+{\color{red}{f(0.5)}}+{\color{red}{f(1)}}+{\color{red}{f(1.5)}}}^{\color{red}{\large\text{heights}}})\cdot \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}{\large\text{width}}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $16$ | $9$ | $4$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A≈(16+9+4+1)\cdot 0.5=15\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068797 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f3cd5193-df6c-5672-95df-52f56264b423" "question-84844930-f95f-5f3a-8037-4adc201a50fc" "question-fd327109-8d69-58f0-a86a-7b3b70080707" "question-9be6577c-8d1d-5823-8ae8-eea53999e09f" "question-247e80ec-6b94-56ac-94f4-78dcaa13b56f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068640 :question/problem "The table below gives some values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the interval $[-4,2].$ If the left Riemann sum approximation of the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ with $3$ equal subintervals has a value of $28,$ then what must be the value of $k?$

| $x$ | $-4$ | $-2$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $3$ | $k$ | $2$ |" :question/worked-solution "The area $\mathcal{A}$ can be approximated using the formula for the left Riemann sum:

$$
\mathcal A\approx(\overbrace{{\color{red}{f(-4)}}+{\color{red}{f(-2)}}+{\color{red}{f(0)}}}^{\color{red}{\large\text{heights}}})\cdot \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}{\large\text{width}}}
$$

So, we set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $-4$ | $-2$ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $3$ | $k$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(5+3+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =(8+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =16+2k\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are given that $\mathcal A$ must be $28,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}16+2k & =28 \\ 2k & =12 \\ k & =6.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068798 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2a6ffc0a-296f-5d33-ab74-d79dec06ff68" "question-b8274948-1d4b-57b0-9024-c09c00401038" "question-8bc09582-a4d5-5866-bf69-244d81d8d845" "question-7e9c9afd-571f-54f0-b5de-d6a5e5729d5e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068641 :question/problem "Suppose a left Riemann sum is used to approximate the area under the curve $y=f(x)=(2x-4)^2$ over the interval $[0,2].$ Is the resulting estimation an overestimate or an underestimate?" :question/worked-solution "Let's sketch our situation. $$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(-3)+f(-1)+f(1))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+k+4)\cdot 2 \\  & =(5+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =10+2k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are given that $A$ must be $4$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}10+2k & =4 \\ 2k & =-6 \\ k & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d71bc7f8-343e-57a7-96e4-46b5c22b0949"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d71bc7f8-343e-57a7-96e4-46b5c22b0949" :answer-field/id #uuid "d71bc7f8-343e-57a7-96e4-46b5c22b0949" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-52b56205-1df3-51bc-8170-ccb928677b3b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9681dbd2-1094-52d5-b2bd-83e405cca6a9" "answer-45fc19c2-908b-50ae-ba05-376e1cbaa786" "answer-52b56205-1df3-51bc-8170-ccb928677b3b" "answer-6f8030cb-2dd5-50f4-a3eb-3a5316c29433" "answer-0960c82b-6c1b-5b1f-8bf9-41ec598d133a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9681dbd2-1094-52d5-b2bd-83e405cca6a9" :answer/id #uuid "9681dbd2-1094-52d5-b2bd-83e405cca6a9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-45fc19c2-908b-50ae-ba05-376e1cbaa786" :answer/id #uuid "45fc19c2-908b-50ae-ba05-376e1cbaa786" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52b56205-1df3-51bc-8170-ccb928677b3b" :answer/id #uuid "52b56205-1df3-51bc-8170-ccb928677b3b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6f8030cb-2dd5-50f4-a3eb-3a5316c29433" :answer/id #uuid "6f8030cb-2dd5-50f4-a3eb-3a5316c29433" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0960c82b-6c1b-5b1f-8bf9-41ec598d133a" :answer/id #uuid "0960c82b-6c1b-5b1f-8bf9-41ec598d133a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-84844930-f95f-5f3a-8037-4adc201a50fc" :question/id #uuid "84844930-f95f-5f3a-8037-4adc201a50fc" :question/math-academy-id "q-86298" :question/problem "The following table shows the rate of change of a city's temperature over a $10$-hour period, starting at $2\,\text{a.m}.$

If the left Riemann sum approximation of the total change in the temperature from $2\,\text{a.m}$ to $12\,\text{p.m}$ has a value of $26{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ what is the value of $k?$" :question/worked-solution "The area $A$ under the curve $y=T(t)$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{T({t}_{0})+T({t}_{1})+…+T({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(T(2)+T(4)+T(6)+T(8)+T(10))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $T(t)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $2$ | $3$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+k+4+2+3)\cdot 2 \\  & =2(k+10) \\  & =2k+20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total change in the temperature from $2\,\text{a.m}$ to $12\,\text{p.m}.$ Since we are given that the left Riemann sum approximation of the total change in the temperature is $26{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2k+20 & =26 \\ 2k & =6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e817f9ef-3f03-51be-bb7b-0bc236498520"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e817f9ef-3f03-51be-bb7b-0bc236498520" :answer-field/id #uuid "e817f9ef-3f03-51be-bb7b-0bc236498520" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-89cc52d0-7d13-5b28-b988-28ce44b1ddc9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6776dc08-9fdf-51fd-996a-bfab15c3331d" "answer-228eec43-938a-5953-916c-999c2cbbaa37" "answer-89cc52d0-7d13-5b28-b988-28ce44b1ddc9" "answer-a159d0cd-4dba-5b36-b32e-909f05583e6d" "answer-9d78173e-a4fa-5da6-a57c-b9e952b87134"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6776dc08-9fdf-51fd-996a-bfab15c3331d" :answer/id #uuid "6776dc08-9fdf-51fd-996a-bfab15c3331d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-228eec43-938a-5953-916c-999c2cbbaa37" :answer/id #uuid "228eec43-938a-5953-916c-999c2cbbaa37" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-89cc52d0-7d13-5b28-b988-28ce44b1ddc9" :answer/id #uuid "89cc52d0-7d13-5b28-b988-28ce44b1ddc9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a159d0cd-4dba-5b36-b32e-909f05583e6d" :answer/id #uuid "a159d0cd-4dba-5b36-b32e-909f05583e6d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9d78173e-a4fa-5da6-a57c-b9e952b87134" :answer/id #uuid "9d78173e-a4fa-5da6-a57c-b9e952b87134" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-fd327109-8d69-58f0-a86a-7b3b70080707" :question/id #uuid "fd327109-8d69-58f0-a86a-7b3b70080707" :question/math-academy-id "q-86296" :question/problem "John is selling juice at a market stall. $$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(k+2+3)\cdot 2 \\  & =2(k+5) \\  & =2k+10\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$

$$

$$

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-3$ | $5$ | $k$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈((-3)+5+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =(2+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =4+2k.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4+2k & =18 \\ 2k & =14 \\ k & =7.\end{aligned}

![](images/99/99cee7824a157e5a08292ebba9e60a5633c7a2f8a5ebb496fc1d5dbe14f858e3.png)

We can *approximate* the area using, for instance, the area of three rectangles, each with a width equal to $1.$

![](images/8a/8aa7a3f9be8371b1459874cd2cb8c0c4caf1000d76b99d134fb6e806e638c548.png)

So, we find the area of each rectangle and then add them all together.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈\overset{\text{[math]1[/math]st rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(1)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]2[/math]nd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(2)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]3[/math]rd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(3)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}} \\  & =[{1}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{2}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{3}^{2}\cdot 1] \\  & =1+4+9 \\  & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we approximated the area using a **left Riemann sum**, which means that the top-*left* corner of each rectangle touches the curve. 

Because the function is *strictly increasing* over the interval $[1,4],$ the rectangles are entirely *below* the function, which means our approximation is an *underestimate* of the actual area." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186070006 :tutorial/content "If ![](images/9a/9ac10abedf6cecc066a4858ab2859e3c3038a43b10ac3261bd4120d0dc861990.svg) on ![](images/88/88e5bb9f44a0b3bb16a7e0e5461c5cc3f1f0bef907eda396d725caf367f29fb5.svg) the area ![](images/6b/6bd69882ede929379fa9babdf49386dd09138f26cabc6a4d617bbac5e92d21a5.svg) under the curve ![](images/44/44c838deb3fa8e3182fbd9d4a03f964dc2731730559d00328190e9259bf01762.svg) over the interval ![](images/2f/2f2185d0962aceaafb8dbacf7486e61ccafbb77a54e961b33e886dd3b79a20df.svg) can be approximated using a left Riemann sum by calculating the area of each rectangle and adding them together.

![](images/85/8547bd96f866100db3ed28f3f23e3446ab5eff50632c425c23c2916c89f823db.png)

  

We can write this mathematically as

![](images/c9/c92cf3627eeb4798f2f72577c3df4788c311b59b575ccbfa17caf14f39dacff1.svg)

where ![](images/4a/4a4a2bd99240362f13e0954449f58ab1c21ae7d29ffec2a1b2c8f1350f6fbec7.svg) and ![](images/09/0979b76b241c9ddb5f2e3d097811c00175e0f9242fa36cc4bff45e2963c3dd8f.svg) are the endpoints of the interval, ![](images/fb/fb2a8560bbc7122a4dd4f1a0bb9862d4368a63f4b03968884a3a60e7423a852c.svg) is the number of rectangles, and the step size ![](images/bd/bd77198ba2d349a9ae25a0866060aa94624d6e255cabe04e818dc06e755ae85c.svg) is given by
![](images/c9/c9f5c5a2741bae825236da3287d754a2526954e894011ace34f5cde5e65a4b45.svg)

We can simplify by factoring out the ![](images/a7/a7e281a725fb2bff766e9ddb72c85bb6f7a8e7d45de6212372795ba1764d5ddc.svg) which gives the following general formula:

![](images/27/277114008d8847a523fb417695fe2f62a4f7ff08efc0b9b8ea58556029ea9c5e.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069981 :tutorial/content "Whether the left Riemann sum underestimates or overestimates the actual area under a function depends on whether the function is increasing or decreasing.

- If the function $f(x)$ is increasing, then the rectangles fall *below* the function, which means the left Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the actual area under the curve $y=f(x).$

![](images/88/883b1d5faacf246557319e1f2b4fa253a06f657c589b24e5ec27eb35c00528c5.png)

- If the function $f(x)$ is decreasing, then  the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means the left Riemann sum gives an *overestimate* of the actual area under the curve $y=f(x).$

![](images/ab/ab23c5b0d95a6bd78ac337266bb504c63b528d756548cbcd38e8b236ef140bc3.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186070007 :tutorial/content "In the last few examples, the step size $\Delta x$ was the same for each of the rectangles. In these cases, we say that the step size is **regular**.

There are situations where the step size can vary, which we call an **irregular step size**. But we can still use a left Riemann sum to approximate the area.

For example, let's use a left Riemann sum to approximate the area under the curve of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ whose data is given in the table below.

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3.5$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $4$ | $6$ | $12$ |

First, note that the domain of $f(x)$ has been *partitioned* as 

$$
\eqalign{
 [1,4] &= [1, 2] \cup [2, 3.5] \cup [3.5, 4] .
}
$$

 

Let's plot what this function might look like, using the values given in the table. 

![](images/2e/2e8563480f46ff335042c3c52a6f60983f871dccb886c8cf3ca0844504a73db6.png)

  

We've drawn some rectangles to help us calculate our left Riemann sum, and we have chosen the heights of each rectangle to be calculated using the left endpoint of each interval. 

By calculating the area of each rectangle, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

![](images/8f/8f62020b1888f7479665b04028acb822fdccfa9049a37e306ea30ce0aa703ac7.svg)

Plugging our numbers into the above, we find

$$
\eqalign{
\mathcal{A}	&\approx	{\color{red}1} \cdot ({\color{blue}2-1})
						+ {\color{red}4} \cdot ({\color{blue}3.5-2})
						+ {\color{red}6} \cdot ({\color{blue}4-3.5}) \[5pt]
			&= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}1} +{\color{red}4} \cdot {\color{blue}1.5}+ {\color{red}6} \cdot {\color{blue}0.5}  \[5pt]
			&=1+6+3\[5pt]
			&= 10.
}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069000 :activity/expected-seconds 1200.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069582 :step/math-academy-id 652096 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069584 :step/math-academy-id 652097 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069583 :step/math-academy-id 652098 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069720 :step/math-academy-id 652101 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069722 :step/math-academy-id 652104 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069721 :step/math-academy-id 652105 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069585 :step/math-academy-id 652108 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069586 :step/math-academy-id 652109 :db/ensure [:step/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-c354aefb-fffc-5ecc-8cac-e2625bd63b47" :question/id #uuid "c354aefb-fffc-5ecc-8cac-e2625bd63b47"] ["question-c354aefb-fffc-5ecc-8cac-e2625bd63b47" :question/math-academy-id "q-334744"] ["question-c354aefb-fffc-5ecc-8cac-e2625bd63b47" :question/problem "Which of the following global truncation error expressions represent a fourth-order numerical method?

I. $e(Δx)=4(Δx)^{4}+2(Δx)^{7}$

II. $e(Δx)=11(Δx)^{4}+0.5(Δx)^{5}$

III. $e(Δx)=0.2Δx+6(Δx)^{4}$"] ["question-c354aefb-fffc-5ecc-8cac-e2625bd63b47" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

With that in mind, let's check each option in turn:

- For $e(Δx)=4(Δx)^{4}+2(Δx)^{7},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $4(Δx)^{4}.$
So, statement I corresponds to an order $4$ method.

- For $e(Δx)=11(Δx)^{4}+0.5(Δx)^{5},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $11(Δx)^{4}.$
So, statement II corresponds to an order $4$ method.

- For $e(Δx)=0.2Δx+6(Δx)^{4},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $0.2Δx.$
So, statement III corresponds to an order $1$ method.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only"."] ["question-c354aefb-fffc-5ecc-8cac-e2625bd63b47" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["question-87b4272d-ed6b-52ae-b49c-9dfe670380e7" :question/problem "$$

$$

Find the solution to the system of equations given above.

{{field-2}}"] ["question-87b4272d-ed6b-52ae-b49c-9dfe670380e7" :question/worked-solution "To get rid of the fractions in the first equation, we must multiply the first equation by the lowest common denominator of the fractions, which is $12.$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}p-\frac{1}{4}q=3 & |\,\times 12 \\ -4p-7q=4\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}4p-3q=36 \\ -4p-7q=4\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that the $4p$ term in the first equation can cancel with the $-4p$ term in the second equation.

Adding the two equations eliminates the $p$-variable, and allows us to solve for $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{4p}-3q & =36 \\ -\cancel{4p}-7q & =4 \\ -10q & =40 \\ q & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $q=-4$ into the equation $-4p-7q=4$ to solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-4p-7q & =4 \\ -4p-7\cdot (-4) & =4 \\ -4p+28 & =4 \\ -4p & =-24 \\ p & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $p=6$ and $q=-4.$"] ["question-87b4272d-ed6b-52ae-b49c-9dfe670380e7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{3x}+8y & =-24 \\ -\cancel{3x}+y & =-30 \\ (8y+y) & =(-24-30) \\ 9y & =-54 \\ y & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=-6$ into the first equation to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+8y & =-24 \\ 3x+8(-6) & =-24 \\ 3x-48 & =-24 \\ 3x & =24 \\ x & =8\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5x+2y=1 \\ \frac{2x}{3}-\frac{y}{9}=-1 & |\,\times 9\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}5x+2y=1 \\ 6x-y=-9\end{aligned}

We will use the substitution method to solve the system. Let's solve for $y$ in the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-y & =-9 \\ 6x+9 & =y \\ y & =6x+9\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can substitute $y=6x+9$ into the first equation and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+2y & =1 \\ 5x+2(6x+9) & =1 \\ 5x+12x+18 & =1 \\ 17x+18 & =1 \\ 17x & =-17 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of $y,$ we substitute $x=-1$ into the equation $y=6x+9,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =6x+9 \\  & =6(-1)+9 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

["question-cb34e92b-11ce-5586-a6db-ed20acf39bd8" :question/math-academy-id "q-216062"] ["question-cb34e92b-11ce-5586-a6db-ed20acf39bd8" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3}s-\frac{2}{3}t=-1 \\ s+\frac{1}{4}t=2\end{aligned}
$$

Find the solution to the system of equations given above."] ["question-cb34e92b-11ce-5586-a6db-ed20acf39bd8" :question/worked-solution "To get rid of fractions, we multiply the first equation by $3$ and the second equation by $4,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3}s-\frac{2}{3}t=-1 & |\times 3 \\ s+\frac{1}{4}t=2 & |\times 4\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}5s-2t=-3 \\ 4s+t=8\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the substitution method to solve the system. Notice that the second equation can easily be solved for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4s+t & =8 \\ t & =8-4s\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $t=8-4s$ into the first equation and then solve for $s:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5s-2t & =-3 \\ 5s-2(8-4s) & =-3 \\ 5s-16+8s & =-3 \\ 13s & =13 \\ s & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of $t,$ we substitute $s=1$ into the equation $t=8-4s$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =8-4s \\  & =8-4(1) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $s=1$ and $t=4.$"] ["question-cb34e92b-11ce-5586-a6db-ed20acf39bd8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] \{\begin{aligned}a+\frac{3}{5}b=\frac{9}{5} \\ \frac{3}{7}a+\frac{1}{7}b=1\end{aligned}

Find the solution to the system of equations given above."] ["question-0f1e5457-cea5-5c5a-997b-b02818578f46" :question/worked-solution "To get rid of fractions, we multiply the first equation by $5$ and the second equation by $7,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}a+\frac{3}{5}b=\frac{9}{5} & |\times 5 \\ \frac{3}{7}a+\frac{1}{7}b=1 & |\times 7\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}5a+3b=9 \\ 3a+b=7\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the substitution method to solve the system. Notice that the second equation can easily be solved for $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3a+b & =7 \\ b & =7-3a\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $b=7-3a$ into the first equation and then solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5a+3b & =9 \\ 5a+3(7-3a) & =9 \\ 5a+21-9a & =9 \\ -4a & =-12 \\ a & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of $b,$ we substitute $a=3$ into the equation $b=7-3a$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =7-3a \\  & =7-3(3) \\  & =7-9 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $a=3$ and $b=-2.$"] ["question-0f1e5457-cea5-5c5a-997b-b02818578f46" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "answer-field-172d876b-a2ec-53c9-b98d-a6ec2ea0fdc4"] [17592186096637 :knowledge-point/questions "question-0f1e5457-cea5-5c5a-997b-b02818578f46"] [17592186097919 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we might have a system of equations with fractional coefficients, such as the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y=-4 \\ 7x-5y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

We can turn the system into an equivalent system involving only integer coefficients. This will make it easier to solve.

In general, we multiply each equation by its lowest common denominator. In this instance, multiplying the first equation by the lowest common denominator of the fractions $(4)$ will do the job:

![](images/7f/7ff92bdf3b9c8bf5ffb571d598788f37bcd698f7b3971c337531bf9fe7f55e4e.svg)

Now, we can solve the system using, for example, the elimination method. Notice that the $5y$ term in the first equation can cancel with the $-5y$ term in the second equation.

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable, and allows us to solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\cancel{5y} & =-16 \\ 7x-\cancel{5y} & =-2 \\ 9x & =-18 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=-2$ into the equation $7x - 5y= -2$ to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}7x-5y & =-2 \\ 7(-2)-5y & =-2 \\ -14-5y & =-2 \\ -5y & =12 \\ y & =-\frac{12}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-2, \,y=-\dfrac{12}{5}.$"] [17592186096853 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0] ["question-ac06f66c-0484-5c24-8d99-9d11ac2dbda8" :question/id #uuid "ac06f66c-0484-5c24-8d99-9d11ac2dbda8"] ["question-ac06f66c-0484-5c24-8d99-9d11ac2dbda8" :question/math-academy-id "q-81048"] ["question-ac06f66c-0484-5c24-8d99-9d11ac2dbda8" :question/problem "Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)=-2{x}^{2}+ey-{e}^{y},$ and determine which of the following statements is true."] ["question-ac06f66c-0484-5c24-8d99-9d11ac2dbda8" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2{x}^{2}+ey-{e}^{y}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(-2{x}^{2}+ey-{e}^{y})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4x & e-{e}^{y}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4x=0 \\ e-{e}^{y}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $x,$ we get

$$
-4x=0\,⟹\,x=0.
$$

Solving the second  equation for $y,$ we get

$$
e-{e}^{y}=0\,⟹\,y=1.
$$

Hence, $(0,1)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$   

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4x)=-4\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(e-{e}^{y})=0 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4x)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(e-{e}^{y})=-{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -{e}^{y}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,1)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -e\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,1),$ we get

$$
H(0,1)=det({f}^{″}(0,1))=(-4)\cdot (-e)-{0}^{2}=4e>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(0,0)=({f}^{″}(0,1))_{11}=-4<0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(0,1).$"] ["question-ac06f66c-0484-5c24-8d99-9d11ac2dbda8" :question/difficulty the function $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-4y-4x,$ and determine which of the following statements is true."] ["question-9f714ecf-c225-5f6f-850c-327baa1dc6f6" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-4y-4x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-4y-4x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4 & 2(xy-2)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4=0 \\ xy-2=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
{y}^{2}-4=0\,⟹\,y=\pm 2.
$$

Then, substituting these values into the second equation, we get

$$
y=-2\,⟹\,x=\frac{2}{-2}=-1,\,\,y=2\,\,\,\,\,⟹\,x=\frac{2}{2}=1.
$$

Hence, $(-1,-2)$ and $(1,2)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-4)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-4)=2y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-4)=2y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-4)=2x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2y \\ 2y & 2x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(-1,-2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-1,-2)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(-1,-2),$ we get

$$
H(-1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(-1,-2))=0\cdot (-2)-(-4)^{2}=-16<0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(-1,-2).$

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,2)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(1,2),$ we get

$$
H(1,2)=det({f}^{″}(1,2))=0\cdot 2-{4}^{2}=-16<0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(1,2).$

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has saddle points at $(-1,-2)$ and $(1,2).$"] ["question-9f714ecf-c225-5f6f-850c-327baa1dc6f6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] :question/problem "The function 
$f(x,y)$ 
has the second derivative

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}-2y & 4y-2x \\ 4y-2x & 4x\end{aligned}]
$$

and has a stationary point at $(1,1).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $H(1,1)>0$

II. $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,1)<0$

III. The point $(1,1)$ is a saddle point of $f$"] ["question-22b41189-2cbf-5d3c-9c30-272b9cf4d5e7" :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(1,1),$ we get

$$
H(1,1)=det({f}^{″}(1,1))=(-2)\cdot 4-{2}^{2}=-12<0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,1)=({f}^{″}(1,1))_{11}=-2<0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(1,1)<0,$ the point $(1,1)$ is a saddle point by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-22b41189-2cbf-5d3c-9c30-272b9cf4d5e7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] Consider the vector field $F$ shown above, and let $C$ be the path where the curve is traversed from $A$ to $B.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

III. ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$"] ["question-e8988e8d-780c-5cf1-8b3a-d358392fe42f" :question/worked-solution "Remember that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ gives the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along $C:$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves from $A$ to $B.$

![](images/df/dfec76b47e8508a57e18440a72986bcae8e2bd19559bd0915ea4530e0b08b4f6.png)

 
So, ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- Statement III is false. It's clear from the picture below that if we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then $F$ works against the motion of the particle as it moves from $B$ to $A.$

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statements I is false, while statement II is true. As the particle moves from $A$ to $B,$ the force $F$ works with the particle for $y<0,$ while $F$  works against the particle for $y>0.$ 

![](images/53/537aca6190fc2f3e06e85c0781a8bb461559ef0a7515ee29aca505f9d615f820.png)

 

By symmetry, the contribution to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ for $y<0$ is canceled out by the contribution for $y>0.$ So,

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ is similar to the previous case.

![](images/49/4939f9a22400a7a56eaeacb77d520e522f50aa8378ca1014a19810122e12da51.png)

 

So, ${\int }_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

stretches in the $x$-direction (with invariant $y$-axis) and stretches in the $y$-direction (with invariant $x$-axis).

For example, let's consider a combined stretch transformation that performs stretches in the following sequence:

- a stretch in the $x$-direction with stretch factor $\dfrac{1}{2},$ followed by

- a stretch in the $y$-direction with stretch factor $-\dfrac{1}{2}.$

The functional representation of the combined stretch is given by

$$
(x,y) \mapsto \left(\dfrac{1}{2}x, -\dfrac{1}{2}y\right).
$$

As it turns out, it does not matter which stretch we perform first. But it's often helpful to think of the stretches being applied one at a time.

Let's apply our combined stretch transformation to the polygon below.

![](images/9b/9b0338a600efa76b14397a4d60b6de500daf4e136b2233b6fa4f021f0861fc24.png)

To stretch a polygon, we 

- find the images of the vertices, and then

- draw segments connecting the image vertices.

So, our three vertices $(4,8)$, $(8,-4)$, $(-8,-8)$ are mapped to the following points by the stretch:

$$
\begin{aligned}(4,8) & ↦(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4,\,-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8)=(2,-4) \\ (8,-4) & ↦(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8,\,-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-4))=(4,2) \\ (-8,-8) & ↦(\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-8),\,-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-8))=(-4,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following result:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -5 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -5 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t+2)}\,x(-2) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5(t+2)) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5(t+2)) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5(t+2)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5(t+2))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(5(t+2))\, \\ \,\operatorname{sin}⁡(5(t+2))\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-530f8a57-b248-5ddf-8ae9-a8b808f3a729" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-4e339ad0-7370-56ee-a106-ae32b1e3a838" :answer-field/id #uuid Consider the circle of radius $16$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$  traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(16,0)?$"] ["question-41e7831f-c290-5b73-a0b9-fe7067c749d0" :question/worked-solution "The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$ centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r,0).$

In our case, the radius $r=16.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$"] ["question-41e7831f-c290-5b73-a0b9-fe7067c749d0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-dd164691-a7a0-5f7f-b4dc-78db7c18f818" :answer-field/id #uuid By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$"] ["question-58130b5b-5f37-553e-8991-9f3dd2a84005" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $$

$$
\frac{\text{d}(u\cdot v)}{\text{d}x}={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{{t}^{2}-4t-21}{{t}^{2}+7t+10} \\  & =\frac{(t-7)(t+3)}{(t+5)(t+2)}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{log}_{7}⁡(x+1)}{2} & =1 \\ {log}_{7}⁡(x+1) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $7,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{7}⁡(x+1) & =2 \\ {7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x+1)} & ={7}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x+1)}=x+1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={7}^{2} \\ x+1 & =49 \\ x & =48.\end{aligned}

["question-00bde4d7-2128-56ee-87f4-eb818e9cb4e3" :question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term:

$$
\begin{aligned}-16{log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =-48 \\ {log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =\frac{-48}{-16} \\ {log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $7,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =3 \\ {7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x-128)} & ={7}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x-128)}=x-128.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x-128 & ={7}^{3} \\ x-128 & =343 \\ x & =471.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-00bde4d7-2128-56ee-87f4-eb818e9cb4e3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-25a7aacd-0ade-5f57-a8d3-34286e4a41cf" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-6f3c55a9-3e7c-5106-8273-98cee0c05243" :question/worked-solution "Along the curve, we have

$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$

$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+({sin}^{2}⁡(2t)-{1}^{2})\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6f3c55a9-3e7c-5106-8273-98cee0c05243" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d0258956-1ae0-545c-833f-e715647fb6c5" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-34262fe5-7916-5312-b653-79d60bb7bbe7" :question/worked-solution "Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$

where $C$ is a portion of the helix parametrized by $r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$"] ["question-b34fc554-6133-5c96-98c9-93a11d4b7862" :question/worked-solution "Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=2t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,k \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy-z\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt-z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-2t\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t-4t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9-4t\,dt \\  & =(9t-2{t}^{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(9-\pi )\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b34fc554-6133-5c96-98c9-93a11d4b7862" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-7a2b773f-820b-5bd4-95ab-10a27879c738" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Find the global minimum value of the function $f(x)=2{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}+1$ on the interval $[-2,\frac{1}{2}].$"] ["question-7df7ee25-2f51-5474-8055-7ad2776c92c8" :question/worked-solution "Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=2{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}+1,$ we get

$$
6{x}^{2}+6x,
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}+6x & =0 \\ 6x(x+1) & =0 \\ x & =-1,0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the critical points are $x=-1,0,$ and the endpoints $x=-2,\frac{1}{2}$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2) & =2(-2)^{3}+3(-2)^{2}+1=-3 \\ f(-1) & =2(-1)^{3}+3(-1)^{2}+1=2 \\ f(0) & =2(0)^{3}+3(0)^{2}+1=1 \\ f(\frac{1}{2}) & =2{(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}+3{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1=2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f(-1)=f(\frac{1}{2})=2,$ so the global maximum is $2.$

- The smallest value is $f(-2)=-3,$ so the global minimum is $-3.$

["question-b8cfbdaa-2d28-5714-8504-0797810897ae" :question/math-academy-id "q-344375"] ["question-b8cfbdaa-2d28-5714-8504-0797810897ae" :question/problem "The global maximum value of the function $f(x)=2\sqrt{x+1}$ on the closed interval $0\le x\le 8$ is{{field-1}}."] ["question-b8cfbdaa-2d28-5714-8504-0797810897ae" :question/worked-solution "Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=2\sqrt{x+1},$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

We can see that ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ for all real values of $x$ in the interval. So there is no solution for ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

So, the only critical points are the endpoints $x=0,8$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =2\sqrt{0+1}=2 \\ f(8) & =2\sqrt{8+1}=2\sqrt{9}=6\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f(8)=6,$ so the global maximum is $6.$

- The smallest value is $f(0)=2,$ so the global minimum is $2.$

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=\sqrt{x+4},$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+4}}.
$$

We can see that ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ for all real values of $x$ in the interval. So there is no solution for ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-3) & =\sqrt{-3+4}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ f(5) & =\sqrt{5+4}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$

- The greatest value is $f(5)=3,$ so the global maximum is $3.$

- The smallest value is $f(-3)=1,$ so the global minimum is $1.$

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=0\,⟹\,x=\pi n,
$$

where $n$ is an integer. We discard all solutions except $x=\pi ,$ since it is the only value that belongs to the given interval.

So, the critical points are $x=\pi $ and the endpoints $x=\frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{3\pi }{2}$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ f(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=1 \\ f(\frac{3\pi }{2}) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f(\pi )=1,$ so the global maximum is $1.$

- The least value is $f(\frac{\pi }{2})=f(\frac{3\pi }{2})=0,$ so the global minimum is $0.$

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}.

Notice that

- the $x$-coordinate of $P$ coincides with the cosine of the angle $\theta,$ and

- the $y$-coordinate coincides with the sine of the angle $\theta.$

So, we have

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta.
$$

For this particular triangle, we have

$$
\sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{z}, \qquad \cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{z}, \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}.
$$

When we take $\sin\theta$ and divide it by $\cos\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } & =\frac{y}{z}÷\frac{x}{z} \\  & =\frac{y}{z}\cdot \frac{z}{x} \\  & =\frac{y\cdot z}{x\cdot z} \\  & =\frac{y\cdot \cancel{z}}{x\cdot \cancel{z}} \\  & =\frac{y}{x} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Although this proof is only for acute angles, the identity is true for any angle, provided that $\tan\theta$ is well-defined.

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+\sqrt{2}y)=1,

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+\sqrt{2}y)=\sqrt{2}.
$$

surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+\sqrt{3}y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+\sqrt{3}y)=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{D}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{∬}_{D}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}{e}^{({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}{e}^{{r}^{2}}r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}r{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{e}^{{r}^{2}}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{{e}^{4}-1}{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}({e}^{4}-1)}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}({e}^{4}-1)}{2}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\sqrt{5}({e}^{4}-1)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186415983 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

We find the intersections of the curve and the line by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x-2 & =-2 \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=2$ along the $x$-axis. 

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](images/e7/e785138362c91f9034d90ee9d923fc818cd299b3ee5d6d25eb1bf40cabc2f2b0.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={x}^{2}-2x-2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=-2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,(-2)-({x}^{2}-2x-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(-{x}^{2}+2x)^{2}\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{4}-4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}-{x}^{4}+\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3}\text{ })|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi ([\frac{1}{5}(2)^{5}-(2)^{4}+\frac{4}{3}(2)^{3}\text{ }]-[0]) \\  & =\pi (\frac{32}{5}-16+\frac{32}{3}) \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f0334985-4e7c-56a4-ba8b-035c69ca7733" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-4b052f20-a657-5fb9-97d6-3e43da2ac8be" :answer-field/id #uuid {{field-1}}"] ["question-4017e457-d6e9-5799-a313-b509dcbd530f" :question/worked-solution "First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/ad/ad089d39428498123469a2ac7895f7d04b8b3ff9dac18a1698462bfc7fabae99.png)

Notice that the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=2$ along the $x$-axis.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](images/97/975f68d06bb52e162ad792987899509f4090c03ec1b55af6335982a2951f6bbf.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=4-(x-1)^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=5.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,5-(4-(x-1)^{2})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{(1+(x-1)^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(1+2(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}((x-1)^{4}+2(x-1)^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi (\frac{1}{5}(x-1)^{5}+\frac{2}{3}(x-1)^{3}+x)\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi (\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{3}+2-(-\frac{1}{5}-\frac{2}{3}+0)) \\  & =\pi (\frac{43}{15}+\frac{13}{15}) \\  & =\frac{56\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}

$$

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-3,$ and

$$

$$
y=2{x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}} & =2 \\ y & =8\end{aligned}
$$

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}{[\,(2)-(\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}{(\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}-2)}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}(\frac{y}{2}-4\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}+4)\text{d}y.\end{aligned}

Consider the region bounded by the curve $x=y+1,$ the vertical line $x=4,$ and the horizontal line $y=0,$ as shown in the picture. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=4.$

$V=$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-2f10ec35-272f-563f-8af5-2c0fc2e74c5d" :question/worked-solution "We want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersection of the curve and the line $x=4$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =4 \\ y & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=3$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](images/f9/f9fd1773b9599b1a4b61fc58c854bf998ed147a9707f719a80a3588874c0eb4f.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=y+1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=4.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}[(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}[4-(y+1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(3-y)^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{3}(3-y)^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{3}(0-{3}^{3}) \\  & =9\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2f10ec35-272f-563f-8af5-2c0fc2e74c5d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-3e380c07-676e-5d1a-a447-464aebaba18c" :answer-field/id #uuid "3e380c07-676e-5d1a-a447-464aebaba18c"] ["answer-8f256f46-100c-5687-961a-0d3ebef98f64" :answer/id #uuid "8f256f46-100c-5687-961a-0d3ebef98f64"] ["answer-8f256f46-100c-5687-961a-0d3ebef98f64" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-8f256f46-100c-5687-961a-0d3ebef98f64" :answer/value "9\pi"] ["answer-field-3e380c07-676e-5d1a-a447-464aebaba18c" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-3e380c07-676e-5d1a-a447-464aebaba18c" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-3e380c07-676e-5d1a-a447-464aebaba18c" :answer-field/correct "answer-8f256f46-100c-5687-961a-0d3ebef98f64"] ["answer-field-3e380c07-676e-5d1a-a447-464aebaba18c" :answer-field/choices "answer-8f256f46-100c-5687-961a-0d3ebef98f64"] ["question-2f10ec35-272f-563f-8af5-2c0fc2e74c5d" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-3e380c07-676e-5d1a-a447-464aebaba18c"] [17592186115302 :knowledge-point/questions "question-2f10ec35-272f-563f-8af5-2c0fc2e74c5d"] [17592186116407 :tutorial/content "Consider the region bounded by the curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ the horizontal line $y=1,$ and the vertical line $x=3,$ as shown in the picture below.

![](images/99/990769dd023de72d2cc4caf3e71d161f6af0605962eb20c8a0d71e67a6ff9b95.png)

Let's rotate this region $360^\circ$ about the line $y=1$ to get the solid shown below. How can we find the volume of this solid?

![](images/e1/e12187d889e7389c4d05e5e91245f555aab4e1c2395ef05168cdf0e3f13b6fe3.png)

We can find the volume using the disc method:

$$
V = \pi \int_{a}^{b} \left[ r(x) \right]^2 \:\textrm{d}x
$$

Here, $r(x)$ is the radius of the disc that corresponds to each point $x$ under consideration. 

**Watch out!** Since the axis of revolution is $y=1$ (not $y=0$), we need to account for the change in the corresponding discs' radius. 

The radius is *not* just $\sqrt{x}.$ Rather, the radius is the distance between the line $y=1$ and the function $y=\sqrt{x}.$ 

![](images/d3/d33fec84ada995fe3593132ae1567c591c030ed458e5cd923180bc2204f4fb4e.png)

To find an expression for the radius, we can take the difference between the upper function and the lower function:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(x) & =(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function}) \\  & =(\sqrt{x})-(1) \\  & =\sqrt{x}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can express the volume as the following integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{3}{(\sqrt{x}-1)}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186116408 :tutorial/content "Consider the region bounded by the curve $y=x^2,$ the vertical line $x=1,$ and the horizontal line $y=4,$ as shown in the picture below.

$$

Therefore, the volume is represented by the integral

$$
a(t)=⟨2,2⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(-10,-8)$ and has velocity $⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$"] ["question-581fcb98-ffbb-541a-98a8-b1aad8f2210c" :question/worked-solution "To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2,2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\,\text{d}t,\int 2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+{C}_{1},\,2t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨2(3)+{C}_{1},\,2(3)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨6+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-6$ and ${C}_{2}=-6.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v(t)=⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩.
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t,\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{3},\,{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨-10,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{3},\,(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-10,-8⟩ & =⟨-9+{C}_{3},\,-9+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=1.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-6t-1,\,{t}^{2}-6t+1⟩.
$$"] ["question-581fcb98-ffbb-541a-98a8-b1aad8f2210c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-73458c53-8f94-50f4-87a0-6b7b8f52ee68" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨12{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 12{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (-{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},{e}^{-t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨4({0}^{3})+{C}_{1},{e}^{-0}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-t}+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-1,-4⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-0}+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-4⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=-3.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{4}-1,-{e}^{-t}-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0ad91671-88c2-5e5d-8e1f-e5e0e6fbe489" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b5d207ef-09f8-5f25-8bd3-232e40b6944c" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-f860a2b3-6e2b-5a0c-99c8-165c277a9c9f" :question/problem "Consider a function $z(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{z(t)\}=Z(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f860a2b3-6e2b-5a0c-99c8-165c277a9c9f" :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{6t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s-6),
$$

where 

$$
s-6>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+6.
$$"] ["question-f860a2b3-6e2b-5a0c-99c8-165c277a9c9f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-bc804dd5-b0b8-5b58-8021-28c39a3f98b4" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-a295f504-6868-5fd6-8219-b8135f071992" :question/math-academy-id "q-332061"] ["question-a295f504-6868-5fd6-8219-b8135f071992" :question/problem "Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L\{{e}^{6t}f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$"] ["question-a295f504-6868-5fd6-8219-b8135f071992" :question/worked-solution "The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{6t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $6$ units to the right."] ["question-a295f504-6868-5fd6-8219-b8135f071992" :question/difficulty ["question-3a25fcb4-6a85-5416-8ab8-d6107a3d8b17" :question/problem "Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}}.$ Does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?"] ["question-3a25fcb4-6a85-5416-8ab8-d6107a3d8b17" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt[n]{3}\cdot {n}^{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot \frac{1}{{n}^{n-1/2}} \\  & =1\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{3}}=1.
$$

Since $L=0<1,$ the series converges by the root test."] ["question-3a25fcb4-6a85-5416-8ab8-d6107a3d8b17" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-0f1fd02c-d7d8-5411-85bd-473d05c64e92" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n}\cdot n}{(9+5n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5n\sqrt[n]{n}}{9+5n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\sqrt[n]{n}\cdot \frac{5n}{n})}{(\frac{9}{n}+\frac{5n}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5\sqrt[n]{n}}{(\frac{9}{n}+5)} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 1}{0+5} \\  & =\frac{5}{5} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=1,$ the root test gives no conclusion."] ["question-0f1fd02c-d7d8-5411-85bd-473d05c64e92" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-f5cf7d5d-3952-5581-beaf-679fd852cabd" ["question-d497f3f8-01e4-568d-82c0-af0842ace04d" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{6}^{n}}{{5}^{n}{n}^{6}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{6}^{n}}{{5}^{n}{n}^{6}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{6}{5\cdot \sqrt[n]{{n}^{6}}}) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{\sqrt[n]{n}})}^{6} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\cdot {1}^{6} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=\frac{6}{5}>1,$ the series diverges by the root test."] ["question-d497f3f8-01e4-568d-82c0-af0842ace04d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-af92a5d6-20ee-53fa-be9c-28e2a23392fd" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{8n+1}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{n(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10\sqrt[n]{n}}{(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & =\frac{10\cdot 1}{8+0} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=\frac{5}{4}>1,$ the series diverges by the root test."] ["question-af92a5d6-20ee-53fa-be9c-28e2a23392fd" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(0.5)+f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

| $x$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1.25+2+2.25+2)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =7.5\cdot 0.5 \\  & =3.75\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b62ef58e-043d-550b-83fb-b95a07d27915" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-aa9732c7-7fe4-5d54-92ce-d54efeda2989" :answer-field/id #uuid continuous function $f(x)$ over the closed interval $[-3,3]$ with a regular step size. If the left Riemann sum approximation of the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ with $3$ subintervals defined by the given points has a value of $4$, then what must be the value of $k?$

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $5$ |"] ["question-f3cd5193-df6c-5672-95df-52f56264b423" :question/worked-solution "The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(-3)+f(-1)+f(1))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+k+4)\cdot 2 \\  & =(5+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =10+2k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are given that $A$ must be $4$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}10+2k & =4 \\ 2k & =-6 \\ k & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f3cd5193-df6c-5672-95df-52f56264b423" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d71bc7f8-343e-57a7-96e4-46b5c22b0949" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-84844930-f95f-5f3a-8037-4adc201a50fc" :question/math-academy-id "q-86298"] ["question-84844930-f95f-5f3a-8037-4adc201a50fc" :question/problem "The following table shows the rate of change If the left Riemann sum approximation of the total change in the temperature from $2\,\text{a.m}$ to $12\,\text{p.m}$ has a value of $26{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ what is the value of $k?$"] ["question-84844930-f95f-5f3a-8037-4adc201a50fc" :question/worked-solution "The area $A$ under the curve $y=T(t)$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{T({t}_{0})+T({t}_{1})+…+T({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(T(2)+T(4)+T(6)+T(8)+T(10))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $T(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $T(t)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $2$ | $3$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+k+4+2+3)\cdot 2 \\  & =2(k+10) \\  & =2k+20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total change in the temperature from $2\,\text{a.m}$ to $12\,\text{p.m}.$ Since we are given that the left Riemann sum approximation of the total change in the temperature is $26{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2k+20 & =26 \\ 2k & =6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-84844930-f95f-5f3a-8037-4adc201a50fc" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e817f9ef-3f03-51be-bb7b-0bc236498520" :answer-field/id #uuid {{field-1}}"] ["question-9be6577c-8d1d-5823-8ae8-eea53999e09f" :question/worked-solution "The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+f({x}_{2})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(2)+f(4)+f(6))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the points are $2,4,6,8$ with three subintervals, the step size is

$$
Δx=\frac{8-2}{3}=2.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each left-endpoint:

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-3$ | $5$ | $k$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈((-3)+5+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =(2+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =4+2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are given that $A=18$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}4+2k & =18 \\ 2k & =14 \\ k & =7.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-9be6577c-8d1d-5823-8ae8-eea53999e09f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-094a080c-b2c0-5da9-a43a-31f0cd0dae34" :answer-field/id #uuid "094a080c-b2c0-5da9-a43a-31f0cd0dae34"] ["answer-556a6e29-9fdc-550d-b85c-3606a717e3f5" :answer/id #uuid "556a6e29-9fdc-550d-b85c-3606a717e3f5"] ["answer-556a6e29-9fdc-550d-b85c-3606a717e3f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-556a6e29-9fdc-550d-b85c-3606a717e3f5" :answer/value "7"] ["answer-field-094a080c-b2c0-5da9-a43a-31f0cd0dae34" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-094a080c-b2c0-5da9-a43a-31f0cd0dae34" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-094a080c-b2c0-5da9-a43a-31f0cd0dae34" :answer-field/correct "answer-556a6e29-9fdc-550d-b85c-3606a717e3f5"] ["answer-field-094a080c-b2c0-5da9-a43a-31f0cd0dae34" :answer-field/choices "answer-556a6e29-9fdc-550d-b85c-3606a717e3f5"] ["question-9be6577c-8d1d-5823-8ae8-eea53999e09f" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-094a080c-b2c0-5da9-a43a-31f0cd0dae34"] [17592186068797 :knowledge-point/questions "question-9be6577c-8d1d-5823-8ae8-eea53999e09f"] ["question-247e80ec-6b94-56ac-94f4-78dcaa13b56f" :question/id #uuid "247e80ec-6b94-56ac-94f4-78dcaa13b56f"] ["question-247e80ec-6b94-56ac-94f4-78dcaa13b56f" :question/math-academy-id "q-315696"] ["question-247e80ec-6b94-56ac-94f4-78dcaa13b56f" :question/problem "Maya runs a lemonade stand. ["question-b8274948-1d4b-57b0-9024-c09c00401038" :question/worked-solution "![](images/ad/ad1e85721eb2142f5cad422530aeed86c0919f34261d19e11e9f056cf355b387.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(1.5)+f(2)+f(2.5)+f(3)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $1.5$ | $2$ | $2.5$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3.25$ | $3$ | $2.25$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3.25+3+2.25+1)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =9.5\cdot 0.5 \\  & =4.75\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is *strictly decreasing* over the interval $[1.5,3.5],$ the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means our approximation is an *overestimate* of the actual area."] The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2)+f(2.5)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ | $2.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $1.25$ | $2$ | $3.25$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+1.25+2+3.25)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =7.5\cdot 0.5 \\  & =3.75\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is *strictly increasing* over the interval $[1,3],$ the rectangles reach *below* the function, which means our approximation is an *underestimate* of the actual area."] $$

$$

| $x$ | $0$ | $3$ | $5$ | $7$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δx$ | $3$ | $2$ | $2$ | $3$ | $-$ |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $4$ | $5$ | $9$ | $15$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈1\cdot 3+4\cdot 2+5\cdot 2+9\cdot 3 \\  & =3+8+10+27 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}

"question-6dc2cb61-7e14-5e92-9670-4b835f928971"] [17592186070005 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we wish to find the area $\mathcal{A}$ under the graph of $y=x^2$ between the $x$-values $x=1$ and $x=4,$ as shown below.

![](images/99/99cee7824a157e5a08292ebba9e60a5633c7a2f8a5ebb496fc1d5dbe14f858e3.png)

We can *approximate* the area using, for instance, the area of three rectangles, each with a width equal to $1.$

![](images/8a/8aa7a3f9be8371b1459874cd2cb8c0c4caf1000d76b99d134fb6e806e638c548.png)

So, we find the area of each rectangle and then add them all together.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈\overset{\text{[math]1[/math]st rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(1)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]2[/math]nd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(2)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]3[/math]rd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(3)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}} \\  & =[{1}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{2}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{3}^{2}\cdot 1] \\  & =1+4+9 \\  & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we approximated the area using a **left Riemann sum**, which means that the top-*left* corner of each rectangle touches the curve. 

Because the function is *strictly increasing* over the interval $[1,4],$ the rectangles are entirely *below* the function, which means our approximation is an *underestimate* of the actual area."] [17592186070006 :tutorial/content "If ![](images/9a/9ac10abedf6cecc066a4858ab2859e3c3038a43b10ac3261bd4120d0dc861990.svg) on ![](images/88/88e5bb9f44a0b3bb16a7e0e5461c5cc3f1f0bef907eda396d725caf367f29fb5.svg) the area ![](images/6b/6bd69882ede929379fa9babdf49386dd09138f26cabc6a4d617bbac5e92d21a5.svg) under the curve ![](images/44/44c838deb3fa8e3182fbd9d4a03f964dc2731730559d00328190e9259bf01762.svg) over the interval ![](images/2f/2f2185d0962aceaafb8dbacf7486e61ccafbb77a54e961b33e886dd3b79a20df.svg) can be approximated using a left Riemann sum by calculating the area of each rectangle and adding them together.

![](images/85/8547bd96f866100db3ed28f3f23e3446ab5eff50632c425c23c2916c89f823db.png)

There are situations where the step size can vary, which we call an **irregular step size**. But we can still use a left Riemann sum to approximate the area.

For example, let's use a left Riemann sum to approximate the area under the curve of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ whose data is given in the table below.

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3.5$ | $4$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $4$ | $6$ | $12$ |

First, note that the domain of $f(x)$ has been *partitioned* as

$$
\begin{aligned} [1,4] &= [1, 2] \cup [2, 3.5] \cup [3.5, 4]. \end{aligned}
$$

Let's plot what this function might look like, using the values given in the table.

![](images/2e/2e8563480f46ff335042c3c52a6f60983f871dccb886c8cf3ca0844504a73db6.png)

We've drawn some rectangles to help us calculate our left Riemann sum, and we have chosen the heights of each rectangle to be calculated using the left endpoint of each interval.

Estimate the order of the numerical method." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.08$ to $0.02.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.08}{0.02}=4.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={4}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.13$ to $0.002.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.13}{0.002}=65.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{p+1} & ≈65 \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{4}⁡(65) \\ p+1 & ≈3.011… \\ p & ≈2.011….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is $2.$"} {:db/id 17592186221987 :question/id #uuid "36473f35-3093-5439-832b-c821da150814" :question/math-academy-id
