Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-3)}\,x(3) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6(t-3)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(6(t-3)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6(t-3)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6(t-3))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6(t-3))\, \\ \,\operatorname{sin}⁡(6(t-3))\,\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b0d055da-4dd2-51f2-ae55-dae45284bf27" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482648}} {:db/id 17592186482629 :step/content {:db/id 17592186482509 :question/answer-fields x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,

$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$  

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$  Line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Starting from $\text{L3},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

we evaluate both sides at $t={t}_{0}$ to obtain

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

which is line $\text{L4}.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ $\text{by substituting }t={t}_{0}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Line $\text{L5}$ gives

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c.
$$

Since $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}={I}_{n}$, the right-hand side simplifies to $c$, so

$$
c=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0}).
$$

Simplify once, then apply $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}$, to obtain

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L6}.$ Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-3t} \\ 2{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-(-1))}\,x(-1) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t+1)) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t+1)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t+1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t+1))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t+1)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t+1))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below.

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Since $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}={I}_{n}$, the right-hand side simplifies to $c$, so

$$
c=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0}).
$$

Simplify once, then apply $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}$, to obtain

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L6}.$ Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$

$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}

Power Function"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{1}{3{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{-6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\frac{{x}^{-6+1}}{-6+1})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\frac{{x}^{-5}}{-5})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{15}\cdot {x}^{-5}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{15{x}^{5}}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186233181 :question/id #uuid "4687a896-1912-54fd-bab7-72fd9b8cd442" :question/math-academy-id "q-113734"} {:db/id 17592186233182 :question/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the integral of a power function multiplied by a constant, like $5x^2.$ How do we proceed?

According to the **constant factor rule**, we can just take the constant factor out of the integral, like this:

$$
\int 5 x^2\, \textrm{d}x = 5\cdot \int x^2 \,\textrm{d}x
$$

Then, we solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}5\cdot \int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x & =5\cdot (\frac{{x}^{2+1}}{2+1})+C \\  & =\frac{5}{3}{x}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can use this trick in general. Whenever the integrand is a function $f(x)$ multiplied by a constant $k,$ we can simplify as

$$
\int k f(x)\, \textrm{d}x = k \int f(x) \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

**Watch out!** We can only take *constant factors* out of integrals. We *cannot* take any variables out of integrals." :tutorial/id #uuid "f293df60-4b16-57ab-88c1-d784d4b5e36c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 698 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "![](images/f4/f44fad12ad1f7d465423f92258caae38e0c536153ba2c3c3a6de573061c69993.png)

The quarter-circle above is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x = 6\cos\theta, \qquad y = 6\sin\theta.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $\theta?$" :question/worked-solution "The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

In our case, the radius $r = 6.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=6\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-circle, we associate the parameter $\theta$ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](images/4b/4bd384e2b1a9d0568617ddbfd5ac7dbe9630882b45c40d7912f4809a6e0be551.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta$ to $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right],$ we get the required quarter-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-circle are 

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=6\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186088362 :question/id #uuid "f9ceb55c-d1e9-5689-8032-0bd11852d402" :question/math-academy-id "q-78681"} {:db/id 17592186088368 :question/id #uuid Circle"}] :question/problem "Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=3\cos\theta + 2,\quad y=3\sin\theta - 4, \quad 0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi.
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta.$ We can do this using the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1
$$

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{3} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y+4}{3} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these values into the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2}+(y+4)^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x-2)^2 + (y+4)^2 = 9.$"} {:db/id 17592186049488} {:db/id 17592186526386} {:db/id 17592186088020 :question/id #uuid "e0808c46-a050-5e50-a062-e87353dcdd48" By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =49({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =49(1) \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/math-academy-id 25242} {:db/id 17592186088676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088960 :tutorial/content "The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x= r\cos\theta+a,\quad y=r\sin\theta+b,\quad  \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

For example, the parametric equations of a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(1,-2)$ are

$$
x= 2\cos\theta+1,\quad y=2\sin\theta-2,\quad  \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

These parametric equations traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(3,-2),$ the rightmost point on the curve.

![](images/69/692b62bc09342cae8b8be19f135ecb9e5b98460ad65ee13bfdddf39a7e1a5b6b.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "801f608f-f3d3-5612-9c1f-45d78532f743" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4284 :tutorial/title "The Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point"} :step/id #uuid "ac1e138c-9132-571a-8812-16394c6aaaed" :step/math-academy-id 25994 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088598}} {:db/id 17592186088677 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088961 :tutorial/content "To convert the parametric equations of a circle to a Cartesian equation, we can eliminate the parameter $\theta$ using the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1
$$

To demonstrate, consider the circle defined parametrically as

$$
x=5\cos\theta,\quad y=5\sin\theta, \quad 0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi.
$$

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{5} & =\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & ={sin}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these values into the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}\theta +{sin}^{2}\theta  & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $x^2+y^2 = 25.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ae768e3d-4836-50d3-95b7-d5e142a470fe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4285 :tutorial/title "Converting the Parametric Equations of a Circle to Cartesian Form"} :step/id #uuid "45680d1f-e317-530f-84b4-835f674c3aee" :step/math-academy-id 25995 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088664}}] :activity/title "Parametric Equations of Circles" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186087894} {:db/id 17592186088596 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088925 :tutorial/content "The parametric equations of a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin are

Substituting these values into the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}\theta +{sin}^{2}\theta  & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsinh}⁡x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}}, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}, &  & \,x\in (1,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{artanh}⁡x) & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}, &  & \,x\in (-1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know the derivative of the base inverse hyperbolic functions, we can differentiate combinations of these functions, by using the properties of differentiation.

For example, let's find the derivative of 

$$
y = \arcosh(x^2).
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡({x}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{({x}^{2})^{2}-1}}\cdot {({x}^{2})}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{4}-1}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{2x}{\sqrt{{x}^{4}-1}}.\end{aligned}

$$

Recall that

$$

$$

$$

have

$$
\frac{3t-9}{{t}^{2}+t-12}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{3t-9}{{t}^{2}+t-12} \\  & =\frac{3(t-3)}{(t-3)(t+4)} \\  & =\frac{3\cancel{(t-3)}}{\cancel{(t-3)}(t+4)} \\  & =\frac{3}{t+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the numerator equal to zero, we get $3=0,$ which is a false statement. Therefore, $f(t)=0$ has no solution, and so $f(t)$ has no roots."} {:db/id 17592186054742 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054556 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}g(y) & =\frac{{y}^{3}-2{y}^{2}-25y+50}{{y}^{3}+{y}^{2}-25y-25} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}(y-2)-25(y-2)}{{y}^{2}(y+1)-25(y+1)} \\  & =\frac{(y-2)({y}^{2}-25)}{(y+1)({y}^{2}-25)} \\  & =\frac{(y-2)(y-5)(y+5)}{(y+1)(y-5)(y+5)} \\  & =\frac{(y-2)\cancel{(y-5)(y+5)}}{(y+1)\cancel{(y-5)(y+5)}} &  \\  & =\frac{y-2}{y+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2=0\,⟹\,y=2\end{aligned}
$$

$f(t)=\frac{3t-9}{{t}^{2}+t-12}.$" :question/worked-solution "The roots of $f(t)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(t)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{3t-9}{{t}^{2}+t-12}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{3t-9}{{t}^{2}+t-12} \\  & =\frac{3(t-3)}{(t-3)(t+4)} \\  & =\frac{3\cancel{(t-3)}}{\cancel{(t-3)}(t+4)} \\  & =\frac{3}{t+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the numerator equal to zero, we get $3=0,$ which is a false statement. Therefore, $f(t)=0$ has no solution, and so $f(t)$ has no roots."} :step/id #uuid "268eb4f9-3381-592c-aa6f-741cf272b0a8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186522890}} {:db/id 17592186522837 :step/content {:db/id 17592186522768 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03a4f702-63d6-559a-a0dd-ab624a5eb606" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=4" :db/id 17592186522022} {:answer/id #uuid "27570a30-bc64-5dd2-bf7a-c9dfffda49a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=-2" :db/id 17592186522109} {:answer/id #uuid "3e970e43-56e8-51a7-8b67-1a34c8189d31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=-2,4" :db/id 17592186522154} {:answer/id #uuid "609ca3c1-35ba-50ca-a3f5-8ffaec27d898" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The equation has no real solution" :db/id 17592186522219} {:answer/id #uuid "654e9075-d5c0-5942-8335-3af4eecc1069" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z=2" :db/id 17592186522229}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186522219} :answer-field/id #uuid "88c05edb-27ce-5999-bea1-f451f6da5f5a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186522626}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "afbc25b8-e022-51c1-8f23-554ddf441b28" :question/math-academy-id "q-24662" :question/problem "Solve $g(z)=0$ where $g(z)=\frac{{z}^{2}+4}{{z}^{2}-4}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor $g(z),$ as follows:

\begin{aligned}g(z) & =\frac{{z}^{2}+4}{{z}^{2}-4} \\  & =\frac{{z}^{2}+4}{(z+2)(z-2)}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

:question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find $x$ such that ${log}_{4}(3x-2)=3.$" :question/worked-solution "To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $4,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}(3x-2) & =3 \\ {4}^{{log}_{4}(3x-2)} & ={4}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${4}^{{log}_{4}(3x-2)}=3x-2.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-2 & ={4}^{3} \\ 3x-2 & =64 \\ 3x & =66 \\ x & =22.\end{aligned}

226} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186060563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060906 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the equation $\log_3 x = 4.$ Can we determine $x?$

Recall that the inverse operation of the logarithm is exponentiation. So, to isolate $x,$ we must exponentiate both sides of this equation. 

The base of the logarithm is $3,$ so we use a base of $3$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡x & =4 \\ {3}^{({log}_{3}⁡x)} & ={3}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above may look complicated, but since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $3^{(\log_3{x})}=x.$ Therefore, we get   

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={3}^{4} \\ x & =81.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $x = 81$ is the solution." :tutorial/id #uuid "bbfe9e19-d1ed-5df9-97f9-0e9c7f9f50e9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2810 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad
y(t) = t^2.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048362} {:db/id 17592186048703} {:db/id 17592186180007 :question/id #uuid "fb63c8a6-afef-5638-9fea-8aaeb2054ae5" :question/math-academy-id "q-124594"} {:db/id 17592186180013 $$

$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{t}\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{t})}\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{t}+t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186387595 :question/id #uuid "87d7259c-ca26-53c7-b47d-c8aa49f4ead9" :question/math-academy-id "q-124875" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179675 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}((x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(t-2+{t}^{3}-t)\cdot 1+(t-2+2)\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}-2+3{t}^{3}-t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{t}^{3}-t-2\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}

$$

$$
x(t) =2t, \qquad 
y(t) = \cos t , \qquad 
z(t) = \sin t.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2t)^{3}\cdot (2)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}

$\mathbf{r}(t)=\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 3\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in[0,\pi].$" :question/worked-solution "Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = \cos t, \qquad
y(t) = 3\sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-3{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,dt \\  & =-3{t|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-3\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180285 :question/id #uuid "7db959c5-fcb6-5723-b0e1-39e452e905f4" :question/math-academy-id "q-81170" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179734 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $r(t)=3{t}^{2}\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$" :question/worked-solution "Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=3{t}^{2},\,y(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k \\  & =6t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx-z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt-z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{t}^{2}\cdot (6t)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }18{t}^{3}-9{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }18{t}^{3}-9\,dt \\  & =(\frac{9{t}^{4}}{2}-9t){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =72{\pi }^{4}-18\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186259725 :question/id #uuid "50abec54-f13d-56bf-8342-cf451db15600" :question/math-academy-id "q-124721"} {:db/id 17592186351215 :question/id #uuid for $t\in [0,2].$" :question/worked-solution "Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)={t}^{2},\,y(t)=4t-1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-1)\,j \\  & =2t\,i+4\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(3x+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}((3x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{t}^{2}+4t-1)\cdot 2t+{t}^{2}\cdot 4\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6{t}^{3}+8{t}^{2}-2t+4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6{t}^{3}+12{t}^{2}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}{t}^{4}+4{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{3}{2}(2)^{4}+4(2)^{3}-{2}^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[24+32-4] \\  & =52\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048540} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "43316bd7-4a4d-5b4e-a6f6-c7ace880dd8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "60{\pi {:db/id 17592186180477}} {:db/id 17592186180395 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180681 :tutorial/content "Line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y$ often come in pairs. For example, 

$$
\int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C (x-y) \, \textrm dy.
$$

We usually express a sum of line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y$ as a single integral. In the case above, we can write this sum as

$$
\int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + (x-y) \, \textrm dy.
$$

Let's evaluate this integral in this case where $C$ is given by the line segment

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=\underbrace{(6t+1)}_{x(t)} \,\mathbf{i} + \underbrace{(2t+1)}_{y(t)} \,\mathbf{j}, \qquad t\in\left[0,1\right].
$$

Along the path $C,$ we have

$$
x = 6t+1, \qquad y = 2t+1.
$$

Computing the derivative of $\mathbf r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)\,j \\  & =6\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the line integral by applying a change of variables, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}x+(x-y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x-y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x-y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6t+1+2t+1)\cdot 6+(6t+1-(2t+1))\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8t+2)\cdot 6+(4t)\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}48t+12+8t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}56t+12\,\text{d}t \\  & ={28{t}^{2}+12t|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =28+12 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

As before, we can evaluate this integral by parameterizing the curve $C$ using the parameter $t\in [a,b]$ and then rewriting the integral using a change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f\,\text{d}x+f\,\text{d}y+f\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

We usually express a sum of line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y$ as a single integral. In the case above, we can write this sum as

$$
\int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + (x-y) \, \textrm dy.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)\,j \\  & =6\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the line integral by applying a change of variables, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}x+(x-y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x-y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x-y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6t+1+2t+1)\cdot 6+(6t+1-(2t+1))\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8t+2)\cdot 6+(4t)\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}48t+12+8t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}56t+12\,\text{d}t \\  & ={28{t}^{2}+12t|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =28+12 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=2x-x^2,$ we get

$$
f'(x) = 2-2x,
$$

and solving $f'(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
2-2x = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x=1.
$$

The critical points are $x=1$ and the endpoints $x=-1,4$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1) & =2(-1)-(-1)^{2}=-3 \\ f(1) & =2(1)-(1)^{2}=1 \\ f(4) & =2(4)-(4)^{2}=-8.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f(1)=1,$ so the global maximum value is $1.$

- The least value is $f(4)=-8,$ so the global minimum value is $-8.$

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "For the function $f(x)=3{x}^{4}+8{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-24x+5,$ defined on the closed interval $-2\le x\le 2,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The global maximum value is $45$
- **II.** The global minimum value is $-14$
- **III.** The global maximum value is $18$" :question/worked-solution "Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=3{x}^{4}+8{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-24x+5,$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=12{x}^{3}+24{x}^{2}-12x-24,
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12{x}^{3}+24{x}^{2}-12x-24 & =0 \\ 12({x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-x-2) & =0 \\ {x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-x-2 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}(x+2)-(x+2) & =0 \\ (x+2)({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (x+2)(x-1)(x+1) & =0 \\ x & =-2,\,-1,\,1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the critical points are $x=-2,\,-1,\,1,$ and the endpoints $x=-2,2$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2) & =3(-2)^{4}+8(-2)^{3}-6(-2)^{2}-24(-2)+5=13 \\ f(-1) & =3(-1)^{4}+8(-1)^{3}-6(-1)^{2}-24(-1)+5=18 \\ f(1) & =3(1)^{4}+8(1)^{3}-6(1)^{2}-24(1)+5=-14 \\ f(2) & =3(2)^{4}+8(2)^{3}-6(2)^{2}-24(2)+5=45\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f(2)=45,$ so the global maximum is $45.$

- The smallest value is $f(1)=-14,$ so the global minimum is $-14.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "For the function $f(x)=\frac{{e}^{x}}{x},$ defined on the interval $[\frac{1}{2},2],$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The global maximum value is $\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}$
- **II.** The global minimum value is $2\sqrt{e}$
- **III.** The global minimum value is $4\sqrt[4]{e}$" :question/worked-solution "Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=\frac{{e}^{x}}{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{e}^{x}\cdot x-{e}^{x}\cdot 1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}(x-1)}{{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{e}^{x}(x-1)}{{x}^{2}}=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

So, the critical points are $x=1,$ and the endpoints $x=\frac{1}{2},2$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{1}{2}) & =\frac{{e}^{1/2}}{(\frac{1}{2})}=2\sqrt{e}≈3.3 \\ f(1) & =\frac{{e}^{1}}{1}=e≈2.7 \\ f(2) & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}≈3.7\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f(2)=\frac{{e}^{2}}{2},$ so the global maximum is $\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}.$

- The smallest value is $f(1)=e,$ so the global minimum is $e.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:knowledge-point/title "Discarding Stationary Points of a Function on a Given Interval"}] :question/problem "Find the global maximum and minimum values for the function $f(x) = x^4 - 6 x^2$ on the closed interval $[-1, 3].$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=x^4 - 6x^2,$ we get

$$
f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x,
$$

and solving $f'(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}-12x & =0 \\ 4x({x}^{2}-3) & =0 \\ 4x(x+\sqrt{3})(x-\sqrt{3}) & =0 \\ x & =0,\pm \sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x = -\sqrt 3 \approx -1.73$ does not belong to the interval $[-1,3]$, we ignore this point.

So, the critical points are $x=0,\sqrt{3}$ and the endpoints $x=-1,3$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

Finally, we evaluate $f$ at the critical points:

$$
\eqalign{
		f(-1) 	& = (-1)^4 - 6(-1)^2 = -5\[5pt]
 		f(0) 		& = (0)^4 - 6(0)^2 = 0\[5pt]
 		f(\sqrt 3) 	& = (\sqrt 3)^4 - 6(\sqrt 3)^2 = -9\[5pt]
 		f(3) 		& = (3)^4 - 6(3)^2 = 27 \		
 		}
$$

We conclude that the global maximum is $27$ and the global minimum is $-9.$

:question/worked-solution "Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)={x}^{4}-8{x}^{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =4{x}^{3}-16x,\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}-16x & =0 \\ 4x({x}^{2}-4) & =0 \\ 4x(x-2)(x+2) & =0 \\ x & =-2,\,0,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x=2$ does not belong to the interval $[-3,1]$, the critical points are $x=-2,0,$ and the endpoints $x=-3,1$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-3) & =(-3)^{4}-8(-3)^{2}=9 \\ f(-2) & =(-2)^{4}-8(-2)^{2}=-16 \\ f(0) & =(0)^{4}-8(0)^{2}=0 \\ f(1) & =(1)^{4}-8(1)^{2}=-7\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f(-3)=9,$ so the global maximum is $9.$

- The least value is $f(-2)=-16,$ so the global minimum is $-16.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1) & =3(-1)^{4}-8(-1)^{3}+3=14 \\ f(0) & =3(0)^{4}-8(0)^{3}+3=3 \\ f(1) & =3(1)^{4}-8(1)^{3}+3=-2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f(-1)=14,$ so the global maximum is $14.$

- The least value is $f(1)=-2,$ so the global minimum is $-2.$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "For the function $f(x)=(x-2)^{2}{e}^{x},$ on the closed interval $-1\le x\le 1,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The global maximum value is $\frac{9}{e}$
- **II.** The global maximum value is $4$
- **III.** The global minimum value is $e$" :question/worked-solution "Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=(x-2)^{2}{e}^{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =2(x-2){e}^{x}+(x-2)^{2}{e}^{x} \\  & =(x-2){e}^{x}[2+x-2] \\  & =x(x-2){e}^{x},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
x(x-2){e}^{x}=0\,⟹\,x=0,\,2.
$$

Since $x=2$ does not belong to the interval $[-1,1]$, the critical points are $x=0$ and the endpoints $x=-1,1$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1) & =(-1-2)^{2}{e}^{-1}=\frac{9}{e}≈3.31 \\ f(0) & =(0-2)^{2}{e}^{0}=4 \\ f(1) & =(1-2)^{2}{e}^{1}=e≈2.72\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f(0)=4,$ so the global maximum is $4.$

- The least value is $f(1)=e,$ so the global minimum is $e.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{\pi }{4}+\pi n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is an integer. We discard all solutions except $x=-\frac{\pi }{4}+\pi =\frac{3\pi }{4}$ and $x=-\frac{\pi }{4}+2\pi =\frac{7\pi }{4},$ since they are the only values that belong to the given interval.

So, the critical points are $x=\frac{3\pi }{4},\,\frac{7\pi }{4},$ and the endpoints $x=0,\,2\pi $ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints).

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=-1 \\ f(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})=\sqrt{2} \\ f(\frac{7\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4})=-\sqrt{2} \\ f(2\pi ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )=-1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The greatest value is $f(\frac{3\pi }{4})=\sqrt{2},$ so the global maximum is $\sqrt{2}.$

- The smallest value is $f(\frac{7\pi }{4})=-\sqrt{2},$ so the global minimum is $-\sqrt{2}.$

But how do we find the global extrema of a continuous function on a closed interval $[a,b]?$

We apply the **candidates test**, which consists of the following three steps.

**Step 1**:  Find all of the critical points. The critical points are our "candidates."

- If the function is defined on a closed interval $[a,b],$ then we must remember to include the endpoints as well.

- If the function is defined on an open interval $(a,b),$ then we do not include the endpoints.

**Step 2**: Determine the value of the function at each of the critical points.

**Step 3**: Compare all the values of $f$ found in step $2.$ The greatest of these values is the global maximum value, and the least is the global minimum value." :tutorial/id #uuid The diagram above shows the unit circle. What are the coordinates of the point $P$?" :question/worked-solution "Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta
$$

We're given that

$$
\theta=45^\circ
$$

at the point $P$. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \cos 45^{∘} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \\
y &= \sin 45^{∘} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the coordinates of $P$ are

$$
\left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\right)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049407} {:db/id 17592186050847} {:db/id 17592186055184 :question/id #uuid "8a87a967-d2f1-5692-a90f-293ff19f1dc8" :question/math-academy-id "q-267324"} {:db/id 17592186055444 :question/id #uuid "2c083513-739b-5c7c-9203-acdd46c5a889" :question/math-academy-id "q-64328"} {:db/id 17592186055445 :question/id #uuid "a4854e55-7280-53d4-946f-06eb6eb5be1a" :question/math-academy-id "q-64337"} {:db/id 17592186054717 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054515 :question/id #uuid "59696ddf-7aa4-561a-ac77-2216038294b2" :question/math-academy-id "e-3346"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "568011de-56c0-55f4-95ec-0a426cbf6b67" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049794}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055185 :question/id #uuid "80cce89c-3065-54a5-9310-40ea2f3befb0" :question/math-academy-id "q-267352"} {:db/id 17592186055446 :question/id #uuid "58adfdfb-8a6a-5b73-a9ed-33d397b103fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-64339"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Central Angle Given the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle"} {:db/id 17592186054515 :question/id #uuid "59696ddf-7aa4-561a-ac77-2216038294b2" :question/math-academy-id "e-3346" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054717 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "568011de-56c0-55f4-95ec-0a426cbf6b67" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Central Angle Given the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle"}] :question/problem "![](images/56/56adc0846dcc0a0f6352eb4ce411f4fffdcd6f91e20524c83bd70af1bd4d948c.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $y$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}$, what is the measure of the angle $\theta$?" :question/worked-solution "We're given that

$$
y=\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}
$$

at the point $P$. Therefore, we have

$$
\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}
$$

We compute the angle $\theta$ using the inverse sine:

$$
\theta = \arcsin\left(\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}\right) = 60^\circ
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049794} {:db/id 17592186055185 :question/id #uuid "80cce89c-3065-54a5-9310-40ea2f3befb0" :question/math-academy-id "q-267352"} {:db/id 17592186055446 :question/id #uuid "58adfdfb-8a6a-5b73-a9ed-33d397b103fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-64339" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186054717 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "568011de-56c0-55f4-95ec-0a426cbf6b67" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Central Angle Given the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bbf3e945-915f-505c-8eba-a8b885843931" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "50^{∘}" :db/id 17592186053914} {:answer/id #uuid "bf79e7fe-af5c-50a2-a68d-090ec078fb45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "75^{∘}" :db/id 17592186053915} {:answer/id #uuid "e3c498ac-930e-5a47-94ab-0d0db471847f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "30^{∘}" :db/id 17592186053916} {:answer/id #uuid "f2e00890-fb9e-5664-b8da-34bd2c52b2bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "40^{∘}" :db/id 17592186053917} {:answer/id #uuid "16e8c52d-f083-58c5-9b57-eb7f41ca4a5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "45^{∘}" :db/id 17592186053918}] :answer-field/id #uuid "ad7b8292-2cc9-59fa-8427-59bb85b1cab1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186053913}] :question/problem "![](images/19/198f3a8a98e9650cf53c81a24a4fc96e08a743bdd6c48e47eb4b59f5bc8e4f2c.png)

$$
x=\dfrac{\sqrt 8}{3}
$$

at the point $P$. Therefore, we have

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 8}{3}
$$

$$
\sec\theta = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}
$$

we can calculate $\sec\theta$ as follows:

$$
\sec\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt 8}{3}\right)} =\dfrac{3}{\sqrt 8} = \dfrac{3\sqrt 8}{8}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050928} {:db/id 17592186051029} {:db/id 17592186055169 :question/id #uuid "c6b2510a-bb87-51a6-b0d0-db9132fb7af7" :question/math-academy-id "q-246763"} {:db/id 17592186055449 :question/id #uuid "a64d54c0-06aa-5ce1-ae67-d8a817ea748a" :question/math-academy-id "q-64970"} {:db/id 17592186054719 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054516 :question/id #uuid "ee188df6-0ef5-5819-8fd9-77d48e8a5dce" :question/math-academy-id "e-3347"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83a4297b-016b-5182-bf4f-cd2b64a23c41" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055186 :question/id #uuid "78792848-55be-58c9-9626-95bc5dd9855c" :question/math-academy-id "q-267423"} {:db/id 17592186055448 :question/id #uuid "a4befd6a-01db-5e7a-94ce-f42e69d69717" :question/math-academy-id "q-64969"} {:db/id 17592186410425 :question/id #uuid "56f00061-e4f7-5bf8-94e9-0bb7b8e48e5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-64985"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Tangent or Cotangent of a Central Angle Given a Point on the Unit Circle"} {:db/id 17592186054516 :question/id #uuid "ee188df6-0ef5-5819-8fd9-77d48e8a5dce" :question/math-academy-id "e-3347" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054719 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83a4297b-016b-5182-bf4f-cd2b64a23c41" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Tangent or Cotangent of a Central Angle Given a Point on the Unit Circle"}] :question/problem "![](images/1b/1b084e0ad229e935d70d751f0e0ddaacf5832017951a7ef8e334f27834662d5c.png)

$$

at the point $P$. Therefore, we have

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 7}{7}, \qquad \sin\theta =\dfrac{\sqrt{42}}{7}

$$
\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\cos\theta}
$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186055186 :question/id #uuid "78792848-55be-58c9-9626-95bc5dd9855c" :question/math-academy-id "q-267423"} {:db/id 17592186055448 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186055706 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055959 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the unit circle with a central angle $\theta$ in the first quadrant, measured in the usual way.

![](images/3d/3d51ca417ba4f6f62bd3e5db5997842d0671f18920a7de70578146a49de79ec3.png)

Notice that

- the $x$-coordinate of $P$ coincides with the cosine of the angle $\theta$, and
- the $y$-coordinate coincides with the sine of the angle $\theta$.

So, we have

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta
$$

Consequently, if we know the angle $\theta$, we can easily work out the coordinates of the point $P$, and vice-versa. This works regardless of whether the angle $\theta$ is given in degrees or radians.

For now, we'll focus on points located in the first quadrant. Later, we will encounter points in all quadrants." :tutorial/id #uuid "8e9912a6-a3c6-5076-9724-a53f5e215dd8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2493 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "03f7f3cb-7a44-54e1-965c-a670919e31f2" :step/math-academy-id 453943 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055707}} {:db/id 17592186055707 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054716 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054514 :question/id #uuid "c4d9963b-1fed-523f-89c7-961ffb12feee" :question/math-academy-id "e-3343"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "70b2f3c7-1600-51c6-91ad-855bcee7d18a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049407} {:db/id 17592186050847}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055184} {:db/id 17592186055444} {:db/id 17592186055445}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle Given Its Central Angle"} :step/id #uuid "38d038fc-1d12-524b-b9d7-96c6225df167" :step/math-academy-id 453944 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055708}} {:db/id 17592186055708 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055960 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the unit circle and a point $P(x,y)$ that lies on the circle.

![](images/3d/3d51ca417ba4f6f62bd3e5db5997842d0671f18920a7de70578146a49de79ec3.png)

To prove that

$$
x=\cos\theta
$$

and

$$
y=\sin\theta
$$

let's examine the triangle that's formed by $\overline{OP}$ and the $x$-axis.

![](images/53/53d84bedcddcb484bc613a2f01e002afe16b614daa909ff744195bcc45464472.png)

Notice that:

- The hypotenuse has length $1$ since it is a radius of the unit circle.
- The adjacent and opposite sides have lengths $x$ and $y$, respectively.

Therefore, using the definitions of $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$, we have

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{1} = x, \qquad \sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{1} = y
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e7838544-050b-5270-a16a-1679e3489a02" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2494 :tutorial/title "A Proof of the Unit Circle Property"} :step/id #uuid "8eef6615-9b8a-526e-9e9e-25070edfdad2" :step/math-academy-id 453948 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055709}} {:db/id 17592186055709 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054717 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054515 :question/id #uuid "59696ddf-7aa4-561a-ac77-2216038294b2" :question/math-academy-id "e-3346"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "568011de-56c0-55f4-95ec-0a426cbf6b67" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049794}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055185} {:db/id 17592186055446}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Central Angle Given the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle"} :step/id #uuid "9d51bf5e-1d13-5f8d-9fd6-c02b852842c4" :step/math-academy-id 453949 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055710}} {:db/id 17592186055710 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054718 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054517 :question/id #uuid "acb093c8-daa1-5eee-8678-e985fb9dfd71" :question/math-academy-id "e-3348"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8487f45b-a734-5375-abc2-5a347d49587c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050928} {:db/id 17592186051029}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055169} {:db/id 17592186055449}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratio Given the Coordinates of a Point on the Unit Circle"} :step/id #uuid "a21ae939-d688-510c-9d02-aec18c105046" :step/math-academy-id 453952 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055711}} {:db/id 17592186055711 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055963 :tutorial/content "To find the tangent of an angle using the unit circle, we need to use the relationship

$$
\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}
$$

To see why this is true, let's take a look at the following triangle.

![](images/99/99b51d7d25a266dbfda7839be6bafc335b181ecd6dc74224fcb0557180f872aa.png)

For this particular triangle, we have

$$
\sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{z}, \qquad \cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{z}, \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}
$$

When we take $\sin\theta$ and divide it by $\cos\theta$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sin θ}{\cos θ} &= \frac{y}{z} \div \frac{x}{z} \\
&= \frac{y}{z} \cdot \frac{z}{x} \\
&= \frac{y \cdot z}{x \cdot z} \\
&= \frac{y \cdot z}{x \cdot z} \\
&= \frac{y}{x} \\
&= \tan θ
\end{aligned}
$$

Although this proof is only for acute angles, the identity is true for any angle, provided that $\tan\theta$ is well-defined.

Finally, since

$$
\cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta}
$$

it immediately follows that

$$
\cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}

$$
\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}
$$

To see why this is true, let's take a look at the following triangle.

![](images/99/99b51d7d25a266dbfda7839be6bafc335b181ecd6dc74224fcb0557180f872aa.png)

For this particular triangle, we have

$$
\sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{z}, \qquad \cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{z}, \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}
$$

When we take $\sin\theta$ and divide it by $\cos\theta$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sin θ}{\cos θ} &= \frac{y}{z} \div \frac{x}{z} \\
&= \frac{y}{z} \cdot \frac{z}{x} \\
&= \frac{y \cdot z}{x \cdot z} \\
&= \frac{y \cdot z}{x \cdot z} \\
&= \frac{y}{x} \\
&= \tan θ
\end{aligned}
$$

Although this proof is only for acute angles, the identity is true for any angle, provided that $\tan\theta$ is well-defined.

Finally, since

$$
\cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta}
$$

it immediately follows that

$$
\cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a17ae159-de66-547d-8e9a-2190b512ab3c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2725 :tutorial/title "The Relationship Between Sine, Cosine, and Tangent"} :step/id #uuid "68735c4a-f7f9-5265-80af-ded103195f00" :step/math-academy-id 453955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055712}} {:db/id 17592186055963 :tutorial/content "To find the tangent of an angle using the unit circle, we need to use the relationship

"83bad3df-40e8-5e95-ad95-39947df5a5ac" :topic/math-academy-id 394} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069840 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069945 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a quadratic equation like
$x^2-25 = 0$.
We can solve this equation using the **difference of squares** formula, shown below:

$$
{\color{red}a}^2 - {\color{blue}b}^2 = ({\color{red}a}+{\color{blue}b})({\color{red}a}-{\color{blue}b})
$$

Using the difference of squares formula, we can factor the left-hand side of our quadratic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} - 25 &= 0 \\
x^{2} - 5^{2} &= 0 \\
(x + 5)(x - 5) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we apply the zero product rule to get

$$
x+5=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad x-5=0
$$

which in turn gives

$$
x=-5 \qquad\text{or}\qquad x=5
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-5,5$. We can write this even more concisely as $x=\pm 5$.

**Note:** We could have solved the equation $x^2-25=0$ using the square root method. However, the factoring method introduced in this lesson will become very useful later when we move on to more complicated quadratic equations. Make sure that you learn it!" :tutorial/id #uuid "0e80849d-fec5-5167-8b39-902cd2d825ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1623 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186069840 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069945 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a quadratic equation like
$x^2-25 = 0$.
We can solve this equation using the **difference of squares** formula, shown below:

$$
{\color{red}a}^2 - {\color{blue}b}^2 = ({\color{red}a}+{\color{blue}b})({\color{red}a}-{\color{blue}b})
$$

Using the difference of squares formula, we can factor the left-hand side of our quadratic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} - 25 &= 0 \\
x^{2} - 5^{2} &= 0 \\
(x + 5)(x - 5) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we apply the zero product rule to get

$$
x+5=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad x-5=0
$$

which in turn gives

$$
x=-5 \qquad\text{or}\qquad x=5
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-5,5$. We can write this even more concisely as $x=\pm 5$.

**Note:** We could have solved the equation $x^2-25=0$ using the square root method. However, the factoring method introduced in this lesson will become very useful later when we move on to more complicated quadratic equations. $$
\iint\limits_{S} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{z-x+y^2}} \: \textrm{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=1+x+y^2$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $-1 \leq y \leq 1.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(1+x+y^2\right) = 1,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(1+x+y^2\right) = 2y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z-x+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1+x+{y}^{2})-x+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2(1+2{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106057 :question/id #uuid "cbfa12ab-0e88-552b-be2d-570d6151a60f" :question/math-academy-id "q-160836" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186105887 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7e34a506-206c-5a51-9251-f1cd31df64d4" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Surface Integrals"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c4695a6d-1571-5cef-92fd-65a1424d3c13" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186102229} {:answer/id #uuid "e764e75f-9dc1-5603-8d96-633391ac023a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-12\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186102230} {:answer/id #uuid "20cb5b64-5df2-52a7-b755-66584d125b13" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186102231} {:answer/id #uuid "23c5e819-0177-54dd-995a-3e2f383292b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186102232} {:answer/id #uuid "5ce1b24b-c6d4-5305-bf5a-65da4c5b5093" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-6" :db/id 17592186102233}] :answer-field/id #uuid "6954f89e-46cf-599c-b11b-0656f3bd3e9a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186102228}] :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{z-y}{\sqrt{6}y}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{(2x+y)-y}{\sqrt{6}y}\sqrt{1+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x[\operatorname{ln}⁡y]_{y=1}^{y=e}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =4-1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278491 :question/id #uuid "4c18475c-c837-5db2-8109-d064b9976225" :question/math-academy-id "q-161348" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186105887 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7e34a506-206c-5a51-9251-f1cd31df64d4" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Surface Integrals"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0fb776aa-a231-5b67-b512-2e48959b2c35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "25\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186275612} {:answer/id #uuid "2c72c2e2-f9da-516e-8437-c3433bda72fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{10}{3}" :db/id 17592186275878} {:answer/id #uuid "6b245dba-d742-5bc5-8638-3bc2d09ec996" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "26\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186276438} {:answer/id #uuid "e708156e-7ac2-5ba9-a3f4-3d08a688734d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5+\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186277493} {:answer/id #uuid "fa7e67ad-f360-562e-a7fa-616dede524b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "25+\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186277668}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "6b245dba-d742-5bc5-8638-3bc2d09ec996" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "26\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186276438} :answer-field/id #uuid "7cc0abcd-c9b6-5dbe-9576-78ef1cbd7653" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186277945}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

Coordinates"}] :question/problem "![](images/d8/d8675cb0c59ba915cefe4b0bbe539f1e7e38b5a3ac2fae4bd2bb25e4de96e116.png)

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{S} x^2y \: \textrm{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=\sqrt2x-y$ and whose domain is a semicircle of radius $1$ centered at $O$ in the upper-half plane, as shown above." :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(\sqrt2x-y) = \sqrt2,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(\sqrt2x-y) = -1.
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\cdot \sqrt{1+(\sqrt{2})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\cdot \sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,[\frac{{r}^{5}}{5}]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{15}{[-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{4}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049084} {:db/id 17592186106061 :question/id #uuid "7aed349f-e0e0-5f67-bd76-7726539edfdb" :question/math-academy-id "q-161146"} {:db/id 17592186106062 :question/id #uuid "54f23aef-c157-5234-9df4-3f529af50cc2" :question/math-academy-id "q-161302" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186105888 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "65e5d5ea-f579-5871-924d-075a207c9aa7" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Surface Integrals Using Polar Coordinates"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a61d5324-5c85-5b4b-a79d-899819adb101" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8\sqrt{6}π" :db/id 17592186102259} {:answer/id #uuid "be449c8b-cd10-53ec-8e94-40bfabcd38e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3\sqrt{2}π" :db/id 17592186102260} {:answer/id #uuid "305a627f-325f-5f3b-8d64-02abe4e04896" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186102261} {:answer/id #uuid "6763f6d4-d90a-5fb6-b8ff-43476ed5ac46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}π" :db/id 17592186102262} {:answer/id #uuid "6b361d32-0cbf-55b3-ac4f-abbd90024b0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "π" :db/id 17592186102263}] :answer-field/id #uuid "223d1d79-de5b-5791-9ab7-fa8e90b4871f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186102258}] :question/problem "![](images/78/7836860694ae6246dee36a70b86bc7fcd8cf7358d47a10586ea6880759fb1588.png)

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/92/9215246969b621002a96dec3aed8a012045b8061371e4c6a1234f54d53de29cc.png)

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x+\sqrt{3}y$ whose domain is the circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+\sqrt{3}y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+\sqrt{3}y)=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{D}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{∬}_{D}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}{e}^{({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}{e}^{{r}^{2}}r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}r{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{e}^{{r}^{2}}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{{e}^{4}-1}{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}({e}^{4}-1)}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}({e}^{4}-1)}{2}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\sqrt{5}({e}^{4}-1)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278486 :question/id #uuid "e935e93c-c375-5e87-b42b-951f2a795ef1" :question/math-academy-id "q-161339"} {:db/id 17592186415982 :question/id #uuid What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2-y) = 2x,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^2-y) = -1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(2x)}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,x({x}^{2}-y)\sqrt{2+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,({x}^{3}-xy)\sqrt{2+4{x}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is ${\color{blue} (x^3-xy) \sqrt{2+4x^2}}.$"} {:db/id 17592186050508} {:db/id 17592186050816} {:db/id 17592186530737} {:db/id 17592186106060 :question/id #uuid "7f27ceb2-3e83-5aa6-8caa-7e1929889c49" :question/math-academy-id "q-161106"} {:db/id 17592186106063 :question/id #uuid "c6b7ebb0-3a2c-5e35-8e1b-da3b8793e3c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-161323" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186105889 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8885504f-07fb-5308-a982-608d7baa262b" :knowledge-point/title "Express Surface Integrals as Repeated Integrals"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8797f6aa-cf9f-5cdf-9e2e-81ed04cfb981" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-3\sqrt{10}(x^{2} + xy)" :db/id 17592186102265} {:answer/id #uuid "9aa9edd5-3b13-5153-89a1-cbc230125392" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2\sqrt{10}(-x^{2}y + xy)" :db/id 17592186102266} {:answer/id #uuid "3c94fbac-ac12-5764-97bd-c8d97a316c61" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-10\sqrt{3}(x^{2} - xy)" :db/id 17592186102267} {:answer/id #uuid "4ff3c3f4-ebf9-5068-a4a6-bd8e76178c58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-3\sqrt{5x}(x^{2} + x^{2}y^{2})" :db/id 17592186102268} {:answer/id #uuid "710da267-89b8-50aa-a066-1c9994d5588d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-3\sqrt{5}(x^{2} + 2xy)" :db/id 17592186102269}] :answer-field/id #uuid "83e432a8-15bc-5c76-a70d-b86380fa6c09" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186102264}] :question/problem "Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x, y, z) =-3xz$, where the surface $S$ is defined by $z = \sqrt{2}x + \sqrt{2}y$ for $0 \le x \le 1$ and $0 \le y \le 2$.

"Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{z}^{2},$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=-2x,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=4y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-2x)}^{2}+{(4y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})^{2}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,({x}^{6}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{4}+4{y}^{4}{x}^{2})\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186401226 :question/id #uuid "d8e5c369-0d01-5527-87a6-9d6d08f8cf0d" :question/math-academy-id "q-161314" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186105889 :knowledge-point/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 1264} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186106886 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107153 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D\subseteq \mathbb R^2,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

Now, if a surface is given by the explicit equation $z=g(x,y)$ over a plane region $D$ in Cartesian coordinates, then the canonical parametrization of this surface is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \langle x,\:  y, \: g(x,y) \rangle, \qquad (x,y) \in D.
$$

Moreover, we know that under the canonical parametrization, the magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, for a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D\subseteq \mathbb R^2,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.

that for a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D\subseteq \mathbb R^2,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

Now, if a surface is given by the explicit equation $z=g(x,y)$ over a plane region $D$ in Cartesian coordinates, then the canonical parametrization of this surface is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \langle x,\:  y, \: g(x,y) \rangle, \qquad (x,y) \in D.
$$

Moreover, we know that under the canonical parametrization, the magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, for a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D\subseteq \mathbb R^2,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
